Did You Know the North Star Isn't the Brightest?

Episode 119 of a daily journey through the universe. ⭐
We visit Polaris, the North Star: only around the 48th brightest star, about 430 to 450 light-years away, a triple star, a pulsing Cepheid, nearly fixed above the North Pole, and why Vega will be the pole star in about 12,000 years.

➡️ Tomorrow, Episode 120: Next stop, Sirius. The real brightest star in the night sky.

segments.text: Think the North Star is the brightest star in the sky? It's not even close.
Many people think the North Star is the brightest star in the sky. It's not even close. It's around number forty-eight.
What makes Polaris special is where it sits. Almost exactly above Earth's North Pole.
segments.headline: Above the North Pole

segments.text: As Earth spins, every other star circles around it. Polaris barely moves.
segments.headline: Everything circles it

segments.text: For centuries, sailors and travelers used it to find north. Its height above the horizon even tells you your latitude.
segments.headline: A guide for travelers

segments.text: To find it, follow the two stars at the end of the Big Dipper's cup.
segments.headline: Use the Big Dipper

segments.text: Polaris is about four hundred and thirty to four hundred and fifty light-years away. And it's actually three stars.
The main star is a Cepheid, the blinking kind from yesterday's episode. It pulses about every four days.
segments.headline: It pulses

segments.text: Earth wobbles slowly like a spinning top. In about twelve thousand years, the bright star Vega will be our pole star.
Tomorrow, the true brightest star of the night. And it hides a tiny, super-heavy secret companion. Which part surprised you most? Tell me in the comments, and follow for tomorrow's stop.
